newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian shares close lower on continued dumping.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian shares close lower on continued dumping.

text.p: Steady dumping of leading shares caused the Nigerian stock market to end lower on Tuesday, dealers said.
The index fell to 8536.20 from Monday's close of 8554.1.
Traders said big companies continued to tumble as investors dumped them for smaller ones.

"What we are seeing is an increase in demand for low stocks since the big ones cannot justify their prices," a trader said. He said many investors were now speculating on the small stocks, hoping to profit as they appreciate.
Tuesday's big losers included the big three banks, the leading cement firm, major brewers and troubled oil marketers.
Union Bank fell 20 kobo to 13.10 naira, despite posting a better half-year result to end-March 1997. Profit after tax rose to 452.2 million compared with 427.2 in the comparable period in 1996.
West African Portland Cement Co dipped 25 kobo, closing at 64.20 naira, while conglomerate PZ Industries PZIN.LG, the market's most capitalised firm, ended 19 kobo down at 29.00 naira.
Guinness fell 35 kobo to 6.65 naira and Nigerian Breweries finished 10 kobo weaker at 19.30 naira.

Leading oil marketer National Oil shocked the market with a sharp drop in profit, but its shares closed steady at 60.90 naira. But Agip was still in a freefall, ending at 20.20 naira, 20 kobo down. Texaco continued to rise, in anticipation of a good result, adding eight kobo to 49.70 naira.

Other gains were made mainly in the food sector, were Nestle remained the most attractive stock, adding 25 kobo to 46.25 naira, while Flour Mills rose to 17.30 naira, up 10 kobo. P.S. Mandrides, an oil miller which that its annual profit, rose to 6.10 naira, adding 10 kobo.
BOC Gases, formerly Industrial Gases remained strong on its own impressive results. It added 20 kobo to end at 14.50 naira.
FSB International Bank closed five kobo stronger at 4.50 naira, the same gain as Wema Bank, which finished at 3.10 naira.
The gain of these profitable, but relatively cheaper banks was the loss of the bigger, dearer ones whose shares were selling for well over 10.00 naira, dealers said.
